entries.title: What is OSINT? + A few tools I use and how to use them.
entries.description:
What is OSINT?
Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) is collecting publicly available information on something or somebody. You can find this information from things like social media, public records, and internet faced devices. You can find this into without special access or hacking (all publicly available.) It's used by researchers, journalists, and penetration testers to see an entity's public footprint. Now that you know what OSINT is, I'm going to list some tools and techniques that I use, don't use this on anything you don't have EXPLICIT permission to test on because it can come with severe legal consequences if used improperly.

Google Dorking: While not necessarily a tool, its a technique I love doing.
It involves using specifi, advanced search terms to find overlooked information from websites, here are some common ones.
site:example.com-only results from one domain
filetype:pdf -Finds specific file types
intitle:"index of"-find exposed directory listings
inurl:admin -find login/admin pages (only use with permission)
"exact phrase"-This isn't just limited to OSINT, its been helpful in many other occasions, it only shows results that include your precise wording.

theHarvester-a Linux tool that finds emails, subdomains, and hostnames tied to a domain from public sources. 
Install via pip install theHarvester
theHarvester -d example.com -b google,bing,crtsh (example)
While this is useful for pentesters who need a attack surface mapped (publicly indexed emails and subdomains for that domain) know that it is illegal to use some of the advanced features, and it is highly unethical.

Shodan-Arguably one of the most popular OSINT tools here, Shodan scans the internet and indexes (like Google almost) internet connected devices, servers, webcams, etc. Again, like Google, it uses search filters like port:22, country:US, or product:nginx to narrow your results.

Ethics- While these three are legal because they only surface publicly available info, that doesn't mean it's ethical. Using them against systems or people without authorization can cross legal lines fast, so use this knowledge to understand exposure, not to poke at things that aren't yours.

Thank you to Cullis for recommending the first tutorial.
